Surah al-Ahqaf (The Sand-Dunes)

Meccan, and it has thirty-five verses.

﴿Ha, Mim.﴾ ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the All-Mighty, the All-Wise.﴾ The discussion regarding it is like that which has passed at the opening of the previous surah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 3:

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth﴾ together with what is in them, in terms of their being parts of them and in terms of [creatures] being settled within them.

﴿And what is between them﴾ of the created beings.

﴿Except with truth﴾ is an exceptive (istithna' mufarragh) clause, taken from the most general of the objects (mafa'il), meaning: except as a creation bound up with the truth that wisdom (al-hikmah) requires, both in the cosmic (takwiniyyah) and in the legislative (tashri'iyyah) sense. Or it is taken from the most general of the states (ahwal), either of the subject of "We created" or of its object, meaning: We did not create them in any state except the state of Our being bound up with the truth, or the state of their being bound up with it. It contains, of what is evident, an indication of the existence of the Creator, may He be exalted, of the attributes of His perfection, of the grounding of His actions upon profound wisdoms, and of their culminating in sublime ends.

﴿And a specified term﴾ is conjoined to "the truth" with an elided genitive (taqdir mudaf), meaning: and with the determination of a specified term at which the affair of the whole comes to an end, and that is the Day of Resurrection, the day when the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens [likewise], and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer. It has also been said: it is the last of the period of survival determined for each one. But the words of the Exalted, ﴿And those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾, repel this view, for what they were warned of is the Day of Resurrection, with its complete catastrophe and its general terrors, not the end of their lifetimes. It has also been allowed that "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah) and the clause is circumstantial (haliyyah), meaning: We did not create creation except with truth and with the determination of a term beyond which they will pass, while they do not believe in it and turn away from it and from preparing for it.

﴿قُلْ﴾ (Say), as a rebuke and a silencing of them.

﴿أرَأيْتُمْ﴾ (Have you considered?): inform me. It is also read as "أرَأيْتَكُمْ" (araʾaytakum).

﴿ما تَدْعُونَ﴾ (what you invoke): what you worship.

﴿مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ (besides Allah): i.e., the idols.

﴿أرُونِي﴾ (show me): an emphatic repetition of ﴿أرَأيْتُمْ﴾.

﴿ماذا خَلَقُوا مِنَ الأرْضِ﴾ (what have they created of the earth?): an explanation of the vagueness in "ماذا" (what).

﴿أمْ لَهم شِرْكٌ﴾ (or do they have a share): i.e., a partnership with Allah, exalted is He.

﴿فِي السَّماواتِ﴾ (in the heavens): i.e., in their creation, or in their dominion and governance, such that it might be supposed that they have some trace of a claim to deserve worship. For that which has no part in the existence of anything, in any way whatsoever, is entirely removed from such a claim, even if it were among the living rational beings; so what then is your opinion of the inanimate? ((p-78) marker as in the source.)

Allah's saying ﴿ائْتُونِي بِكِتابٍ﴾ (Bring me a Book) and so on is a rebuke to them by proving them unable to bring a transmitted proof, after their rebuke by their inability to bring a rational proof. That is: bring me a divine Book that exists.

﴿مِن قَبْلِ هَذا﴾ (before this): before this Book, i.e., the Qur'an, which speaks of monotheism and nullifies polytheism, and which indicates the soundness of your religion.

﴿أوْ أثارَةٍ مِن عِلْمٍ﴾ (or a remnant of knowledge): or a remaining trace of knowledge that has been preserved for you from the sciences of the earlier peoples, bearing witness to their deserving worship.

﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ (if you are truthful): in your claim. For it can hardly be sound unless it is supported by a rational proof or a transmitted authority. Since neither of these supports it, and since the proofs of reason and transmission stand against it, its falsity becomes clear.

It is also read as "إثارَةٌ" (ithāratun) with a kasra on the hamza, meaning debate, for it stirs up meanings (yuthīru al-maʿānī). It is also read as "أثَرَةٍ" (athara), meaning something you have been given preference in and singled out for, of hidden knowledge from others than you. It is also read as "إثْرَةٌ" (ithra) with the three vowels and a sukun on the thāʾ. The kasra form means the same as athara (preference). The fatha form is a single occurrence from "athara al-ḥadīth", meaning he transmitted the hadith. The damma form is the name of what is transmitted, like "khuṭba" (sermon), which is the name of what is delivered in a sermon.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 5:

﴿And who is further astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, such as will not respond to him﴾ This is a denial and negation of the possibility that anyone could be equal to the polytheists in misguidance, although the construction of the expression (sabk al-tarkib) negates only that there is anyone more astray than them, without addressing the negation of one equal to them, as has passed more than once. That is: they are more astray than every person who has gone astray, since they abandoned the worship of their Creator, the All-Hearing, the All-Powerful, the Responsive, the All-Aware, in favor of worshipping their own creation, which is devoid of hearing, power, and responsiveness.

﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ This is the limit for the negation of responsiveness.

﴿and they are heedless of their supplication﴾ The first pronoun refers to the object of "yad'u" (calls upon), and the second refers to its subject. The plural in both is in consideration of the meaning of "man" (whoever), just as the singular in what preceded is in consideration of its wording.

﴿are heedless﴾ The plural is used for them, though they are inanimate objects, because the pronouns of rational beings (al-'uqala') are used for them by treating them as rational beings, and because they are described with what has been mentioned of not responding and of heedlessness, despite the clarity of their condition, in order to mock them and their worshippers, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿If you call them, they will not hear your call﴾, and the verse.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 6:

﴿And when mankind is gathered﴾ at the arising of the Resurrection.

﴿they will be enemies to them, and they will be disbelievers in their worship﴾ That is, they will be denying [them] through the tongue of their state or through speech, according to what is related: that God, exalted is He, will give life to the idols, and they will disavow the worship of their worshippers. It has also been permitted that by "them" is meant everything worshipped besides God, including the angels, the jinn, humans and others. The return of the pronouns, and the attribution of enmity and disbelief to them, is then based on *taghlib* (the prevalence of one group over another in grammatical expression). What is meant by this is their disavowal of those [worshippers] and of their worship. It has been said: the pronoun in "they were" refers to the worshippers, and this is their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 7:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾, clear or made clear.

﴿Those who disbelieve say of the truth﴾, i.e., concerning it and about it. The "truth" refers to the recited verses, and it is placed in the position of their pronoun to specify their truthfulness and the obligation of believing in them, just as the relative pronoun is placed in the position of the pronoun referring to those to whom they are recited, to record upon them complete disbelief and misguidance.

﴿when it comes to them﴾, i.e., at the very first moment it comes to them, without reflection or contemplation.

﴿This is clear magic﴾, i.e., its being magic is evident.

(p-79) ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) and a transition from narrating their earlier shamelessness to narrating something even more shameful. The interrogative hamza in "am" (or) is for censure in the form of denial, which implies wonder; that is: "Rather, do they say that he has invented the Qur'an?"

﴿Say: If I have invented it﴾ on the assumption (of that).

﴿then you cannot avail me anything against Allah﴾ since there is no doubt that He, exalted is He, would hasten to punish me then. How, then, would I dare to invent a lie against Him, exalting myself to a punishment from which there is no escape?

﴿He knows best what you plunge into﴾ that is, what you rush headlong into, of disparaging the revelation of Allah, attacking His signs, and calling them sorcery at one time and fabrication at another.

﴿Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you﴾ since He bears witness for me to truthfulness and the delivery (of the message), and against you for lying and denial. This is a warning of the recompense for your plunging (into falsehood). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ is a promise of forgiveness and mercy for whoever repents and believes, and an indication of Allah's forbearance toward them despite the magnitude of their crimes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 9:

﴿Say: I am not an innovation among the Messengers.﴾ Al-bid' (بِدْع): in the sense of al-badi' (البديع), like khil (خِل) in the sense of khalil (خَلِيل), meaning one who has no like or equal. It was also read with a fatha on the dal (بِدَعٍ), as a descriptive adjective like qiyam and zim, or as a plural with an implied annexed noun, meaning "one possessing innovations." This is also permitted in the first reading as a verbal noun (masdar). The disbelievers used to propose to him, peace be upon him, strange signs and ask him about unseen matters out of obstinacy and arrogance. So he was commanded, peace be upon him, to say to them: I am not a unique (badi') among the Messengers, one able to do what they cannot, so that I bring you everything you propose and inform you of everything you ask about of the unseen. For those Messengers before me, peace be upon them, did not bring anything except the signs that God Most High gave them, and they did not inform their people except of what was revealed to them.

﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you.﴾ That is: I do not know what will befall us in the time to come, of God Most High's acts, and what will be decreed for us of matters. It is reported from al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, that it means: I do not know what my affair and your affair in this world will come to. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it means what will be done with me or with you in the Hereafter. It is said that this verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿That God may forgive you your former and latter sins﴾. It is also said that what is negated may be detailed knowledge. The more evident and more suitable view, in line with the occasion of revelation mentioned, is that "ma" refers to matters whose knowledge is not among the duties of prophethood, namely worldly events and occurrences, not what will happen in the Hereafter, for knowledge of that is among the duties of prophethood, and explicit revelation has come with its details concerning what will be done to both parties. Moreover, it is reported from al-Kalbi that the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said to him, and they had become weary of the harm of the polytheists: "How long shall we remain in this state?" He said: ﴿I do not know what will be done with me or with you. Shall I be left in Mecca, or shall I be commanded to leave for a land of palm trees and trees, which has been shown to me and which I have seen?﴾ meaning in his dream. It is permitted that "ma" be a relative pronoun, and the interrogative sense is more fitting to the context of disclaiming knowledge. The repetition of "la" (لا) serves to recall the negation that extends to it and to emphasize it. It was also read "ma yaf'alu" (مَا يَفْعَلُ), with the verb attributed to His pronoun, Exalted is He.

﴿I follow only what is revealed to me.﴾ That is: I do only the following of what is revealed to me, in the sense of restricting his actions, peace be upon him, to following revelation, not restricting following to revelation alone as is the immediate understanding. Its verification has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am. It was also read "yuha" (يُوحَى) with the active voice (يُوحِي), and this is an answer to their demand that he inform them of unseen matters that have not been revealed to him, peace be upon him. It is said that it responds to the Muslims' eagerness to be rid of the harm of the polytheists. The first is more suitable in light of His saying: ﴿And I am only a warner﴾ warning you of the punishment of God Most High according to what is revealed to me.

﴿Clear⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ (mubin)﴾: clear in warning, through manifest miracles.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 46, verse 10:**

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if it is from Allah"﴾ meaning: what is revealed to me of the Qur'an.

﴿from Allah﴾, not sorcery or fabrication as you claim. His words, exalted is He, ﴿and you disbelieved in it﴾ are a *hal* (circumstantial clause, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) with *qad* implied, referring back to the pronoun in the predicate. It is placed between the parts of the conditional (*shart*) to hasten the charge of disbelief against them. Alternatively, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with *kana* (the verb "if it is"), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if it is from Allah, then you disbelieved in it"﴾. However, this is not on the basis that its structure falls within the conditional that is uncertain, whether it occurred or not, in their view, considered in itself. Rather, it is considered in terms of the status of the thing coordinated with it in their view. Their disbelief in it is certain in their view as well. What is uncertain for them is only whether that is disbelief in what is from Allah, exalted is He, or not. The same applies to His words, exalted is He: ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ and the two verbs that follow it, since all of these are matters certain in their view. What is uncertain for them is whether they are a testimony and a belief in what is from Allah, exalted is He, and an arrogance toward it. The meaning is: tell me, if this is in reality from Allah, and you disbelieved in it, and a witness of great standing from the Children of Israel, who is aware of the affairs of Allah, exalted is He, and the secrets of revelation through what was given to them of the Torah, testified.

﴿to its like﴾, meaning: to the like of the Qur'an, from the meanings contained in the Torah, which agree with what is in the Qur'an regarding monotheism, promise, threat, and other matters. For they are in reality the very same as what is in it, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾. The "likeness" is in terms of their being conveyed in other expressions, or it is "to the like of what was mentioned", namely that it is from Allah, exalted is He, and the likeness refers to what was mentioned. It has also been said that *mithl* (like) is a *sila* (relative complement, the part completing a relative construction), and the *fa'* (then) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿then he believed﴾ indicates that he hastened to believe in the Qur'an when he knew that it is of the kind of revelation that speaks the truth. This refers to 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who, when he heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina, came to him, looked at his noble face, knew that it was not the face of a liar, and considered him carefully, and became certain that he was the awaited Prophet. He then said to him: "I will ask you about three things that none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food eaten by the people of Paradise? And does the child resemble its father or its mother?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for the first sign of the Hour, it is a fire that will gather people from the east to the west. As for the food of the people of Paradise, it is the extra piece of the liver of a fish. As for the child, if the man's water precedes, the child resembles him, and if the woman's water precedes, the child resembles her." He said: "I bear witness that you are truly the Messenger of Allah." Then he stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, the Jews are a people of slander. If they learn of my Islam before you ask them about me, they will slander me before you." The Jews came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "What sort of man is 'Abdullah among you?" They said: "He is the best of us, the son of the best of us, our master, the son of our master, and our most learned, the son of our most learned." He said: "What do you think if 'Abdullah becomes Muslim?" They said: "May Allah protect him from that." Then 'Abdullah came out to them and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." They said: "He is the worst of us, the son of the worst of us," and they disparaged him. He said: "This is what I was afraid of, O Messenger of Allah, and what I was wary of." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the earth that he is one of the people of Paradise, except for 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and concerning him was revealed: ﴿and a witness testified﴾, the verse." It has also been said that the witness is Moses (peace be upon him), and his testimony is in what is in the Torah about the sending of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon them both. This is the view of al-Sha'bi. Masruq said: "By Allah, it was not revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Salam, for the *Ha Mim* (the letters *ḥā' mīm* opening the surah) was revealed in Mecca, and 'Abdullah only became Muslim in Medina." al-Kalbi answered that the verse is Medinan, even if the surah is Meccan.

﴿and you became arrogant﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿a witness testified﴾, and the answer of the conditional (*jawab al-shart*, the apodosis) is omitted. The meaning is: tell me, if it is from Allah, exalted is He, and a witness among the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel testified to it, and believed in it without hesitation, and you became arrogant toward belief in it after this rank, who is more astray than you? This is supported by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if it is from Allah, and you disbelieved in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?"﴾ and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. For the absence of guidance indicates misguidance with certainty, and describing them as wrongdoers serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, for if He, exalted is He, left them without guidance, He would be wronging them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 11:

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾: a narration of another part of their false statements concerning the Mighty Qur'an and the believers in it; that is, the disbelievers of Makkah said.

﴿to those who believed﴾: that is, on their account.

﴿Had it been﴾: that is, that which he (peace and blessings be upon him) brought of the Qur'an and the religion.

﴿a good thing, they would not have preceded us to it﴾: for the lofty matters are not attained by the hands of the base, who are the dregs of the common people, the poor, the freedmen and the herdsmen. They said this supposing that religious leadership is attained through worldly means, just as they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ They overlooked that it is bound to spiritual perfections and inner dispositions, founded upon turning away from the base adornments of this world and wholly turning toward the Hereafter, and that whoever succeeds in it has obtained it in full, while whoever is deprived of it has no share of it. It is said: this was said by Banu 'Amir, Ghatafan, Asad and Ash'ar when Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Aslam and Ghifar embraced Islam. It is said: it was said by the Jews when 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions embraced Islam; but this is refuted by the fact that the surah is Makkan, and there would then necessarily be recourse to the claim that the verse was revealed at Madinah.

﴿And since they have not been guided by it﴾: a adverbial clause (zarf) for an omitted element indicated by what precedes it, and what follows is consequent upon it; that is: and since they have not been guided by the Qur'an, they said what they said.

﴿they will say﴾: not content with denying its goodness.

﴿This is an ancient falsehood﴾: just as they said: ﴿the fables of the ancients﴾. It is said that the omitted element is that their obstinacy became manifest, but this is not the case.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 12:

﴿And before it﴾, i.e., before the Qur'an, is the predicate (khabar) of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Book of Moses﴾. It has been said: the clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive new sentence (mustaʼnafa). Whichever it is, it serves to refute their saying, "This is an ancient lie," and to nullify it, for its being a confirmer of the Book of Moses necessarily establishes its truth.

﴿A guide and a mercy﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to "the Book of Moses," i.e., a guide to be followed in the religion of God, exalted is He, and His laws, just as one follows an imam; and a mercy from God, exalted is He, for whoever believes in it and acts in accordance with its requirements.

﴿And this﴾, the one about whom they say what they say.

﴿is a Book﴾ of great standing.

﴿confirming﴾, i.e., confirming the Book of Moses, which is a guide and a mercy, or confirming what is between its hands of all the divine books. It has also been read in this way.

﴿in a tongue, Arabic﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the Book in "confirming," or from itself, since it is specified by the attribute, and its operator is the meaning of indication (ishara). On the first view, it is "confirming." It has been said: it is an object (maf'ul) of "confirming," i.e., it confirms one who has an Arabic tongue.

﴿to warn those who have done wrong﴾ is connected to "confirming," and within it is a pronoun referring either to the Book, or to God, or to the Messenger (ﷺ). The reading with the second-person ta' (of address) supports the last of these.

﴿and as good tidings for the good-doers﴾ is in the place of the accusative, conjoined to the position (mahall) of "li-yundhira" (to warn). It has been said that it is in the place of the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject, i.e., "and it is good tidings." It has also been said that it is conjoined to "confirming."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ That is: they combined tawhid (the affirmation of the Oneness of God), which is the essence of knowledge, and istiqamah (uprightness and steadfastness) in the matters of religion, which is the goal of action. And "thumma" (then) indicates the distance in rank of action and that its being counted depends upon tawhid.

﴿There is no fear for them﴾ of the befalling of something disliked.

﴿Nor will they grieve﴾ over the loss of something loved. The "fa'" (so) is for the nominal sentence containing the meaning of a conditional, and the purpose is to explain the continuity of the negation of grief, not the negation of the continuity of grief, as the predicate being a present-tense verb might suggest; and its explanation has passed several times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 14:

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by the two sublime attributes mentioned.

﴿They are the companions of the Garden, abiding therein forever﴾: "abiding therein" (khalidin fiha) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun hidden in "companions" (ashab). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as a reward﴾ (jaza'an), is in the accusative case either by means of an implied governing verb, meaning: they are rewarded with a reward (yujza'una jaza'an), or by way of the meaning of what preceded, for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those are the companions of the Garden﴾ carries the meaning of "We have recompensed them."

﴿in recompense for what they used to do﴾: from the good deeds of knowledge (al-'ilmiyya) and action (al-'amaliyya).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 15:**

﴿And We have enjoined upon man﴾ to be good

﴿to his parents, goodness﴾. It is also read as "ḥusnan" (with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ), meaning: that he should act toward them with goodness, i.e., an act that is good, or as if the act were itself goodness because of its great excellence. It is also read with a ḍammah on the sīn (ḥusnan) and with a fatḥah on both letters, meaning: that he should do toward them a good deed, or that We enjoin upon him a good enjoining.

﴿His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. That is, in a state of hardship, or a pregnancy accompanied by hardship, which is difficulty. It is also read with a fatḥah (kurhan), and both are dialectal variants, like al-faqr and al-fuqr (poverty). It has been said: the one with the ḍammah (kurh) is the noun, and the one with the fatḥah (kurh) is the verbal noun.

﴿And his bearing and his weaning﴾: that is, the period of his pregnancy and his weaning, which is al-fiṭām (weaning). It is also read as "faṣluhu," "al-faṣl," and "al-fiṣāl," like al-faṭm and al-fiṭām in form and meaning. What is intended by it is the complete suckling that ends with it. Just as the one who said (poetry) intended by "al-amad" the duration: [Every living thing completes the span of its life, and perishes when its term comes to an end]. ﴿Thirty months﴾, during which she endured hardships and suffered difficulties on his account. This is evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, since the weaning is limited to two full years, as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the suckling﴾, which leaves that much time for the pregnancy. It has been said: perhaps the determination of the minimum period of pregnancy and the maximum period of suckling is because both are fixed, and because the connection of lineage and fosterage is established by them.

﴿Until, when he reaches his maturity﴾: that is, he reaches full strength and his strength and intellect are firmly established.

﴿And reaches forty years﴾. It has been said: no prophet was sent before the age of forty. It is also read: "ḥattā idhā istawā wa balagha ashuddahu" (until, when he attains equilibrium and reaches his maturity).

﴿He says: My Lord, inspire me﴾: that is, grant me inspiration. Its origin is "awliʿnī" (make me fond of), from "awzaʿtuhu bi-kadhā" (I made him keep to such-and-such).

﴿That I may be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾: that is, the favor of religion, or what encompasses it and other things.

﴿And that I may do righteous deeds with which You are pleased﴾. The indefiniteness of "ṣāliḥan" (a righteous deed) is for magnification and abundance.

﴿And make righteousness prevail for me among my offspring﴾: that is, make righteousness flow among my descendants and firmly established within them, as in the saying: [my blade wounds their hamstrings]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah, exalted is He, answered the supplication of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them. He freed nine believers, among them Bilal and ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra, and he did not intend any good thing except that Allah, exalted is He, helped him to achieve it. He also prayed, saying: "And make righteousness prevail for me among my offspring," and Allah, exalted and majestic is He, answered him: none of his children remained except that they all believed. Thus the Islam of his two parents and his children was gathered together for him. His father Abu Quhafa met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abi Bakr met him, and the son of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abu ʿAtīq, met him; all of them met the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. This was not granted to any of the Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them all.

﴿Indeed I have turned to You﴾ from what You do not approve, or from what distracts me from remembering You.

﴿And indeed I am among the Muslims﴾, those who have sincerely devoted themselves to You.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 16:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to "the human being," and it is in the plural because what is meant is the category (jins) of people characterized by the attribute described before it. The sense of distance contained in it is to indicate the loftiness of their rank and the elevation of their station. That is: ﴿those﴾ who are described by the noble qualities that have been mentioned.

﴿from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ of acts of obedience, for what is permissible (mubah) is good, but one is not rewarded for it.

﴿and overlook their evil deeds﴾. It is also read with both verbs in the first-person plural (nataqabbalu and natajawazu), attributing them to God Most High, and also read with both verbs in the passive voice. The word "best" (ahsan) is in the nominative, as it stands in the place of the subject (na'ib al-fa'il), and likewise the prepositional phrase.

﴿among the companions of the Garden﴾ That is: being among their number, included in their ranks.

﴿a true promise﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing what is implied by His saying "We accept" and "We overlook": it is a promise from God Most High to them of acceptance and overlooking.

﴿which they were promised﴾ through the tongues of the Messengers.

﴿Those who say to their parents﴾ when they call him to faith.

﴿Fie upon you both!﴾ It is a sound that a person makes when he is annoyed. The *lam* (ل) in ﴿لَكُما﴾ serves to specify the one for whom the exclamation is made, as in *hayta laka* (هَيْتَ لَكَ, "come, I am at your service"). It is also read *uffin* (أُفٍّ) with a fatha and with a kasra, without tanwin, and with the three vowel patterns with tanwin. The relative pronoun (الَّذِي, "the one who") refers to a category of people who speak that speech, and for this reason it is described with a plural, as was mentioned before. It is said: it refers to the disbelieving son who is disobedient to his parents and denies the Resurrection. It is related from Qatadah that it describes a wicked servant who is disobedient to his parents and wicked toward his Lord. As for what is narrated, that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, before his conversion to Islam, this is refuted by the later words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect﴾, and the verse that follows, for he was among the most excellent of the Muslims and their leaders. Al-Siddiqah, may Allah be pleased with her, has denied whoever said that.

﴿Do you both promise me that I will be brought forth?﴾ That I will be raised from the grave after death. It is also read *akhruja* (أَخْرُجَ) from *al-khuruj* (الخُرُوجِ, "to come out").

﴿And generations have passed away before me﴾ and none of them was raised.

﴿While they both call upon Allah for help﴾ they ask Him to grant him relief and to guide him to faith.

﴿Woe to you!﴾ That is, saying to him, "Woe to you!" In origin it is a curse upon him for destruction (*thubur*), but it is intended here to urge and incite him toward faith, not as a literal wish for his ruin.

﴿Believe! Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ That is, the Resurrection. They attributed it to Him, the Exalted, to affirm the truth and to alert him to his error in attributing the promise to them both. It is also read *inna wa'da Allahi* (إنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ) meaning: "Believe that the promise of Allah is true."

﴿But he says﴾ denying them both.

﴿This is nothing﴾ that you call the promise of Allah.

﴿but the fables of the ancients﴾ their falsehoods which they inscribed in books, with no reality behind them.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones who make these statements.

﴿Upon whom the word has come due﴾, which is His saying to Iblis (Satan): ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever of them follows you, all together."﴾ As His saying indicates: ﴿among the communities of jinn and humans that passed away before them﴾. Its tafsir (exegesis) has already been explained in Surat Alif Lam Mim al-Sajdah.

﴿Indeed they﴾, all together,

﴿were losers﴾. They squandered their original innate disposition (fitrah), which is like the capital of their wealth, by following Satan. The sentence gives the reason for the ruling by way of isti'naf (resumptive sentence) of the confirmatory type.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 19:

﴿And for each﴾ of the two groups mentioned.

﴿are degrees according to what they did﴾: these are ranks of recompense for what they did of good and evil. The word "degrees" (darajat) is predominant for the ranks of reward, and its use here is by way of predominance (taghlib).

﴿And that He may pay them in full their deeds﴾: that is, the recompense for their deeds. It has been read with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), i.e., "We pay."

﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ by diminishing the reward of the first group or increasing the punishment of the second. The clause is either a emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) for the act of paying in full, or a resumptive statement (istitnaf) confirming it. The lam (in liyuwaffiyahum) is connected to a deleted element placed later, as if it were said: "that He may pay them in full their deeds and not wrong them their rights." He did what He did, namely determining the recompenses according to the measures of their deeds, and so He made the reward and the punishment into levels.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 46, verse 20:**

﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾: that is, they will be tormented by it. This is from their saying: "The captives were exposed to the sword," meaning they were killed. It is also said that the Fire is presented to them, by way of inversion (al-qalb, a transposition of the grammatical roles of the subject and object), for emphasis.

﴿You squandered your good things﴾: that is, it will be said to them. This is the element that governs the adverb of time (al-nasib lil-zarf, the word that grammatically governs the temporal adverb). It was also read as "أأذْهَبْتُمْ" ( particularly, with two hamzas and an alif between them), as an interrogative of rebuke (al-istifham al-tawbikhi), meaning: "Did you obtain or take what was written for you of the portions and pleasures of this world?"

﴿in your life of the world and you enjoyed them﴾: so nothing of them remained for you after that.

﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾ (p-85): that is, the humiliation (al-hawan). It was also read in this way. ﴿for what you were doing in the world﴾.

﴿you were arrogant in the earth without right﴾: without any entitlement to that.

﴿and for what you used to defy﴾: that is, you went out of obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: because of your arrogance and your persistent defiance. It was also read as "تَفْسِقُونَ" with a kasra on the sin (siyn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 21:

﴿And mention﴾, i.e., to the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿the brother of 'Ad﴾, i.e., Hud (peace be upon him).

﴿when he warned his people﴾: an idafa-substitution (badal al-ishtimal) from it, i.e., at the time of his warning them.

﴿in al-Ahqaf﴾: the plural of ḥiqf (ahqaf, "dunes"), which is a long, raised sand dune with a curve in it, from ihqawqafa al-shay' (meaning "it became bent" or "it curved"). The 'Ad were people of pillars (ʿumud) who lived among sand dunes overlooking the sea, in a land called al-Shajar, from the lands of Yemen. It was also said: between 'Uman and Mahra.

﴿And warners had already passed away﴾, i.e., messengers, plural of nadhir in the sense of mundhir (warner).

﴿before him﴾, i.e., before him in time.

﴿and after him﴾, i.e., after him in time. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) that confirms what came before it and emphasises the necessity of acting upon the requirement of the warning. It was placed between "warned his people" and his saying:

﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾, hastening to what has been mentioned of confirmation and emphasis, and as an announcement that they share in the reported expression. The meaning is: mention to your people the warning of Hud to his people concerning the consequence of shirk and the great punishment. Messengers who came before him and those who came after him likewise warned their peoples, so mention them. As for making it a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "warned," in the sense that he (peace and blessings be upon him) warned them and said to them: "Worship none but Allah, ﴿I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾," and he had informed them that the messengers sent before him and those who would be sent after him were all warners with a warning like his, then, along with what it contains of the strain of supplying the notion of informing, there is necessarily, in attributing "passed away" to those who came after him among the messengers, the treatment of the one yet to come as though he had already passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 22:

﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away﴾ i.e., to turn us away (ta'fikana: taṣrifa-na)﴿ from our gods﴾ from their worship.

﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of the great punishment.

﴿If you are among the truthful﴾ in your promise that it will descend upon us.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 23:

﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with Allah"﴾ That is, regarding the time of its descent, or the knowledge of all things, of which this is one.

﴿with Allah﴾ alone. I have no knowledge of the time of its descent, nor any role in bringing about its coming and occurrence. Its knowledge is only with Allah, the Exalted, so He will bring it to you at its appointed time.

﴿And I convey to you that with which I have been sent﴾ among the duties of the messengership, of which is clarifying that the punishment will descend if you do not desist from polytheism, without having knowledge of the time of its descent. It has also been read as "ublighukum" (ابلغكم), from al-iblagh (conveying).

﴿But I see you to be a people who are ignorant﴾ in that you propose to me what is not among the functions of the messengers, namely bringing the punishment and specifying its time.

The fa' in His exalted words ﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْهُ﴾ ("So when they saw it") is the fa' of faṣīḥa (the fa' that signals an implied elided clause).

The pronoun [in "rawhu," "they saw it"] is either unspecified (mubham), clarified by His exalted words ﴿عارِضًا﴾ ("a cloud"), which is either a tamyīz (specifier) or a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), or it refers back to what they sought to hasten by their saying: ﴿فائْتِنا بِما تَعِدُنا﴾ ("bring us what you threaten us with"). That is: He came to them, so when they saw it, a cloud appearing on the horizon of the sky, ﴿مُسْتَقْبِلَ أوْدِيَتِهِمْ﴾ ("facing their valleys"), meaning heading toward their valleys. The genitive construction here is verbal (lafẓiyya), as in His exalted words: ﴿قالُوا هَذا عارِضٌ مُمْطِرُنا﴾ ("They said: This is a cloud bringing us rain"). For this reason they both came as descriptive adjectives of an indefinite noun.

﴿بَلْ هُوَ﴾ ("Rather, it is...") means: Hūd said. It has also been read thus, and it has been read "qul" ("say"). It is a rebuttal to them, meaning: the matter is not as you think; rather, it is [what you asked for].

﴿ما اسْتَعْجَلْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ ("what you were hasty about") refers to the punishment.

﴿رِيحٌ﴾ ("a wind") is either a substitute (badal) for "mā," or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

﴿فِيها عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾ ("in it is a painful punishment") is a description of "rīḥ," and likewise His exalted words:

﴿Tudammiru﴾, that is, destroys.

﴿kulla shay'in﴾ (everything): their souls and their properties.

﴿bi-amri rabbihā﴾ (by the command of its Lord). It is also read as "yudammiru kulla shay'in" from dammara dammāran, meaning "to perish." In that reading the returning pronoun to the described noun is either omitted, or it is the hā' in "rabbihā." It is also permissible for the clause to be a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) (a new sentence that begins a fresh statement), showing that every contingent thing has a decreed end tied to the command of its Creator. In this case the hā' refers to "kulla shay'in," because it carries the sense of "al-ashyā'" (things). The mention of the command, the Lord, and the attribution to the wind contains, beyond doubt, an indication of the greatness of His majesty, glory be to Him.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-aṣbaḥū lā yurā illā masākinuhum﴾ (so they became such that nothing could be seen but their dwellings), is explanatory (faṣīḥa) (a fa' that signals an implied intermediate step). That is: the wind came upon them and destroyed them, so they became such that nothing could be seen but their dwellings. It is also read as "tarā" with the taʾ and with "masākinuhum" in the accusative, addressed to everyone who is capable of seeing, as an admonition that their condition was such that if everyone came to their lands, they would see nothing there but their dwellings.

﴿kadhālika﴾ (thus), that is, like that dreadful punishment.

﴿najzī al-qawma al-mujrimīn﴾ (We recompense the criminal people). The details of the story have already passed in Surat al-A'rāf. It has been narrated that the wind would lift the tent and the litter-camel woman (ẓaʿīna) into the air until they appeared like a locust. It was said: the first of them to see the punishment was a woman who said: "I saw a wind in which were sparks like shooting flames of fire." It has also been narrated that the first thing by which they recognized that it was a punishment was that they saw what was in the desert of their camp-gear and livestock being carried by the wind between the sky and the earth. So they entered their houses and locked their doors, but the wind uprooted the doors, threw them down, and Allah, exalted is He, tilted al-Aḥqāf (the sand dunes) over them, so they remained beneath them for seven nights and eight days, moaning. Then the wind lifted from them, took them up, and cast them into the sea. It has also been narrated that when Hūd, peace be upon him, sensed the wind, he drew a line around himself and the believers, beside a spring that gushes forth. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Hūd and those with him withdrew into an enclosure, so the wind did not reach them except as a gentle breeze on the skin that the souls found pleasant, while it passed over ʿĀd with their litter-camels between the sky and the earth and struck them with stones.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 26:

﴿And indeed We had established them﴾ That is: We made the 'Ad firmly established, or We empowered them. And "ma" in His saying, ﴿in that wherein We had established you﴾, is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a qualifying noun (mawsufah), and "in" is negative; that is: in that which, or in something which, We had established you in, of abundance, expansiveness, long lives, and all the means of disposing of affairs, as in His saying, ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth in a way We have not established you?﴾ What makes the placement of "in" here appropriate (p-87) is escaping the repetition of the word "ma", which is the reason for changing its alif into a ha' in "mahma" and making it a conditional or extra particle, something not fitting to the context.

﴿And We made for them hearing, sight and hearts﴾ so that they would use them for what they were created for, and know through each of them what its knowledge was tied to of the varieties of blessings, and derive proof through them of the affairs of the One who gave them, Mighty and Majestic, and persist in thanking Him.

﴿But their hearing did not avail them﴾ in that they did not use it for listening to revelation and the admonitions of the messengers.

﴿nor their sight﴾ in that they did not behold through it the created signs set out in the pages of knowledge.

﴿nor their hearts﴾ in that they did not use them to know God, Exalted.

﴿anything﴾ That is: any availing at all. And "min" is extra for emphasis. His saying, Exalted: ﴿since they used to deny the signs of God﴾ is related to "did not avail", and it is an adverbial of time that functions in the manner of causation, insofar as the judgment is based on what it is attached to. Your saying "I honored him since he honored me" is equivalent to your saying "I honored him because of his honoring me, when you honored him, at the time of his honoring." So you honored him in it because his honoring was present in it; likewise the situation with "hayth".

﴿And there encompassed them what they used to mock﴾ of the punishment which they were hastening in the manner of mockery, saying: "Bring us what you promise us, if you are among the truthful."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 27:

﴿And We certainly destroyed what was around you﴾ of towns, O people of Makkah.

﴿Of the towns﴾, like the dwelling place of Thamud, and the towns of the people of Lut.

﴿And We varied the signs﴾, We repeated them for them.

﴿That they might return﴾, so that they would turn back from what they were in of disbelief and sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 28:

﴿So why did those whom they took as gods besides Allah, as a means of approach (qurban), not help them?﴾ Qurban: that by which one draws near to Allah, the Exalted. One of the two objects of "ittakhadhu" (they took) is the omitted relative pronoun, and the second is "alihah" (gods), while "qurbanan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). The meaning is: "Why did they not help them and rescue them from the punishment, those whom they took as gods while they were being drawn near to Allah, the Exalted, since they used to say: 'We worship them only so that they bring us near to Allah in closeness, and these are our intercessors with Allah.'" This contains mockery of them. There is no room for making "qurbanan" a second object with "alihah" as a substitute (badal) for it, because the meaning is then corrupt. For although the substitute is the intended element, in a substitution other than badal al-ghalat (substitution by error) the sentence must remain sound without it, and there is no doubt that our saying "they took them besides Allah as qurban", meaning "as something by which one draws near", is definitively unsound, because He, the Exalted, is the One drawn near to, not the One by which one draws near. So it cannot be correct that they took them as qurban, transgressing Allah in that. It was also read "qurubanan" with a damma on the ra'.

﴿Rather, they strayed from them﴾ That is: they were absent from them. This contains another mockery of them, as if their not helping was due to their absence, or: they were lost to them, meaning their loss from them became manifest entirely. It was said: their help was impossible, like the help of one absent from the one who is being helped.

﴿And that﴾ That is: the loss of their gods from them and the impossibility of their help.

﴿Their falsehood﴾ That is: the result of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods, the outcome of their polytheism. It was also read "afakuhum," and both are verbal nouns, like "al-hidhr" and "al-hadhar." It was read "afakahum" in the past tense, in which case "dhalika" refers to the taking, meaning: that taking, which is its fruit and consequence, turned them away from the truth. It was read "affakahum" with shaddah for emphasis, and "aafakahum" from the verb (af'al), meaning: made them liars. It was read "afikuhum" in the form of the active participle, with a pronoun suffix, meaning: their statements are falsehood, as one says "qawlun kadhib" (a false statement).

﴿And what they used to fabricate﴾ This is coordinated with "ifkuhum," meaning: and the result of their fabricating against Allah, or the result of what they used to fabricate against Him, the Exalted. It was also read "wa dhalika ifkun mimma kanu yaftarun," meaning: that is some of the falsehood among what they used to fabricate.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 29:**

﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾: We inclined them towards you and brought them round towards you. It is read "ṣarrafnā" with the doubled letter, for intensification, because they were a group. This is the reason the pronoun is plural in His words, ﴿listening to the Qur'an﴾, and what follows it. The phrase ﴿listening to the Qur'an﴾ is a *ḥāl muqaddara* (a circumstantial qualifier anticipated in meaning) relative to "nafaran" (a group), since it specifies it by a description. Or it is another description of it. That is: mention to your people the time when We turned towards you a group of the jinn, existing among the jinn, with their listening to the Qur'an anticipated.

﴿When they attended it﴾: i.e., the Qur'an, at the time of its recitation, or the Messenger (ﷺ) at the time of his reciting it to them, by way of *iltifāt* (a shift in grammatical person or address). The first is the more apparent.

﴿They said﴾: i.e., some of them said to others.

﴿Be silent﴾: i.e., be quiet so that we may hear it.

﴿When it was concluded﴾: i.e., completed and finished from its recitation. It is also read in the active voice, with the subject being the pronoun of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. This supports the pronoun in "ḥaḍarūhu" referring to him, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾: intending to warn them upon their return to them. It is narrated that the jinn used to eavesdrop, and when the sky was guarded and they were pelted with meteors, they said: "This is only because of some event that has occurred." Seven men, or six men, of the nobles of the jinn of Nusaybin or Nineveh, among whom was Zawba'a, rose up and set out until they reached Tihama. Then they pressed on to the valley of Nakhla, where they came upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was standing in the depth of the night praying, or during the Fajr prayer, and they listened to his recitation. That was on his return from Ta'if. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them. Rather, he was reciting in his prayer, and they passed by him and stopped to listen while he was unaware of them, so Allah informed him of their listening. It has also been said: rather, Allah commanded him to warn the jinn and recite to them, so He turned towards him a group of them, whom He gathered for him. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I have been commanded to recite to the jinn tonight, so who will follow me?" He said it three times, and they remained silent except for Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: "We set out until, when we were at the top of Mecca, in the Shi'b al-Hajun, he drew a line for me and said: 'Do not leave it until I return to you.' Then he began the Qur'an, and I heard a great commotion until I feared for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Many dark figures covered him and came between me and him, until I could no longer hear his voice, peace and blessings be upon him. Then they dispersed like pieces of cloud. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Did you see anything?' I said: 'Yes, men, black, clothed in white garments.' He said: 'Those were the jinn of Nusaybin.'" They were twelve thousand. The surah he recited to them was ﴿"Read in the name of your Lord"﴾.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 46, verse 30:

﴿They said﴾, that is, upon their return to their people.

﴿O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Musa (Moses)﴾. It is said they said this because they were upon Judaism. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the jinn had not heard of the matter of 'Isa ('Isa, peace be upon him).

﴿confirming what came before it﴾. They meant by it the Torah (al-Tawrah).

﴿guides to the truth﴾, from the correct beliefs ('aqa'id).

﴿and to a straight path﴾ leading to it, which is the laws (shara'i') and righteous deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 31:

﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him﴾ They meant by it what they had heard of the Book, and they described it as a call to Allah the Exalted after having described it as guidance to the truth and the straight path, because the two are inseparable. They called them to that after explaining its truth and its uprightness, as an encouragement for them to respond. Then they reinforced it with their saying:

﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ That is, some of your sins, namely that which was in the pure right of Allah the Exalted, for the rights of people (ḥuqūq al-'ibād) are not forgiven by faith alone.

﴿And will protect you from a painful punishment﴾ prepared for the disbelievers. It is disputed whether they will have a reward other than this or not, and the most apparent view is that they are, in terms of reward and punishment, in the same position as the children of Adam.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 32:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah, he cannot escape [Allah's will] on earth﴾ is an obligation to respond by way of intimidation, following its obligation by way of encouragement, and a confirmation that they are warners, and the mention of "the caller of Allah" explicitly, without being satisfied with one of the two pronouns, is for the sake of emphasis in the obligation, by increasing the affirmation, cultivating awe, and instilling fear. The restriction of inability to escape to being "on earth" is to widen the scope; that is: he cannot escape from Allah, Exalted is He, by fleeing, even if he flees every escape route from its regions or enters into its depths. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he has no protectors other than Him﴾ is an explanation of the impossibility of his being saved through another, following the explanation of the impossibility of his being saved by himself. The plural of "protectors" (awliya', ﴿أولياء﴾) is in consideration of the meaning of "whoever" (man), so it is of the type of matching a plural with a plural, since the individuals are divided into individuals, just as the plural in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾ (ulaika) is, with that consideration, i.e., those characterized by not responding to the caller of Allah.

﴿In manifest error﴾, i.e., its being error is evident, such that it is not hidden from anyone, [for] they turned away from responding to one of this description.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 33:

﴿Do they not see﴾ The hamzah (interrogative particle) here expresses denial, and the waw (conjunction) is for coordination with an implied element that the context calls for. The seeing is of the heart, meaning: Did they not reflect and did they not know with a certain knowledge that approaches direct observation and witnessing?

﴿That Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ originating them without any pattern to imitate or any rule to follow.

﴿and was not wearied by their creation﴾ meaning: He did not tire, nor was He exhausted by it at all, or He was not unable to do it. It is said: "ʿayītu bi-l-amr" (I was at a loss regarding the matter) when its way is not known. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿able﴾ (bi-qādir) is in the place of nominative case, because it is the predicate of "anna" (that), as the reading without the letter bāʾ indicates. The reason for its entering in the first reading is that the negation occurring at the beginning of the verse includes "anna" and what falls within its scope, as if it were said: Is Allah not able?

﴿to give life to the dead﴾ Therefore the question is answered by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yes, indeed He is over all things competent﴾, affirming the power in a general manner that serves as a proof for the intended meaning.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 46, verse 34:

(p-90)﴿And the day those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire﴾: this is an adverb of time (zarf) whose governing verb is an implied "say," whose content is ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾. This is on the basis that the demonstrative refers to what they witness at that time, as such, without any word signifying it occurring to the mind, let alone its masculine or feminine form, since that is befitting its awfulness and magnitude. This has been discussed in Surat al-Ahzab. It has also been said: it refers to the punishment. In this there is mockery of them and rebuke for their derision of God's promise and threat, and for their saying: "We shall not be punished."

﴿They will say: "Yes, by our Lord!"﴾: He emphasized their answer with an oath, as if they hoped to be saved by acknowledging its truth, as they did in the world; but how could they?

﴿He will say: "Taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve."﴾ In it, in the world. The meaning of the imperative is humiliation of them and rebuke of them. The fa' (particle "then") in His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 46, verse 35:

﴿So be patient, as the steadfast of the messengers were patient﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: since the outcome of the matter of the disbelievers is what has been mentioned, then be patient over what afflicts you from their side, as those of firm resolve and determination among the messengers were patient, for you are among their number, indeed among their elite. The "min" here is for specification (tabyin). By "those of firm resolve" (ulu al-'azm) are meant the bearers of sacred law (ashab al-shara'i') who strove to establish and affirm them and were patient in bearing their hardships and in confronting those who attacked them. The most famous of them are Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, upon them be prayers and peace. It has also been said: they are those who were patient under God's trial, like Nuh, who was patient under the harm of his people, who would beat him until he fainted; and Ibrahim, who was patient under the fire and under the slaughter of his son, and the one to be slaughtered was patient under the slaughter; and Ya'qub, under the loss of his son and his sight; and Yusuf, under the well and the prison; and Ayyub, under affliction; and Musa, to whom his people said: "Indeed we are overtaken," and he said: "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me"; and Dawud, who wept over his sin for forty years; and Isa, who did not place one brick upon another. May the blessings of God the Exalted be upon them all.

﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾, that is, for the disbelievers of Makkah, for the punishment is about to descend upon them.

﴿As if, on the day they see what they are promised﴾, of the punishment,

﴿they had not remained﴾ in the world

﴿except for an hour﴾, a brief one,

﴿of a day.﴾ Because of what they witness of the severity of the punishment and the length of its duration. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A message﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this with which you have been admonished is sufficient as an admonition, or it is a delivery of the message from the Messenger. This is supported by the reading "balagha" (he delivered), and it has been read "balaghan" (a delivery), meaning: they delivered a delivery.

﴿So will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾, that is, those who depart from heeding this admonition or from obedience. It has been read with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the lam, and with fatha on both, from halika and halaka, and with the nun of majesty from the causative (ihlak), and with the people in the accusative and as its description. From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ahqaf, ten good deeds will be written for him, equal to the number of every grain of sand in the world."
